To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the holographic theories we study can be characterized by two exponents γ and δ, and that there is a region in the (γ,δ) plane where the holographic theory is a Mott insulator at T=0, while at low temperatures, it is a bad metal with linear resistivity.

the holographic theories with the charge density fully back-reacted on, are generically not insulators at low enough temperatures, the DC resistivities are generically not linear in temperature, and the DC resistivities do not scale as heat capacities.

(1) In holography, the DC resistivities of the charge carriers at low temperature scale as the heat capacity and entropy, (2) The entropy of charged black holes at zero temperature is zero, (3) At low temperature, holographic theories generically have a linear DC resistivity, (4) At low temperature and frequency, the AC conductivity is generically independent of frequency.

the study of holographic models of strongly coupled quantum matter at low temperatures and finite charge densities.
holographic theories of strongly interacting systems at strong coupling, with a focus on their low-temperature properties.
the IR properties of charged holographic theories in the context of condensed matter applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the holographic approach to condensed matter systems at strong coupling is very useful and powerful, and that it is capable of capturing the interplay of the charge density and the most relevant scalar operator, but that the theory is not complete, and that there are still open issues to be addressed.
the holographic theories we study are not suitable for the description of low-temperature condensed-matter physics, except in a small codimension-one region of the parameter space.
the effective holographic theories are not a good model for condensed matter applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the holographic models considered here are very rich in terms of possible IR dynamics, and can capture a large variety of condensed matter physics phenomena.
the holographic models with γ = δ have the most realistic low-temperature behavior.
there is a large region in the (γ,δ) plane that is consistent with condensed matter physics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IR dynamics of holographic theories is richer than previously thought and that the (γ,δ) parameterization is useful for understanding and classifying the IR dynamics.

there exist effective holographic theories where the IR dynamics can be tuned to capture the low-temperature behavior of a wide variety of condensed matter systems, including those where the carriers are massive.
